questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests per-namespace scoping, ConfigMap-driven config, and a small policy engine. Exercises InitContainers, Secrets, PVC logging, and network boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace Deployment
- ConfigMap-driven configuration
- Lightweight policy checks (privilege, caps, readOnlyRootFilesystem)
- InitContainer with jq/curl
- Secret-based tokens and PVC-backed logs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy scope

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: namespace-scanner
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: namespace-scanner
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: namespace-scanner
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-progress curl jq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: scanner
        image: myrepo/namespace-scanner:latest
        env:
        - name: PORTAL_URL
          value: "https://compliance-portal/api/v1/scan"
        - name: TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: compliance-portal-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: compliance-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test this policy in CI?
- How would you handle retries and idempotence when posting digests?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests practical CKAD skills: dynamic configuration via ConfigMaps, per-namespace isolation, InitContainers, health checks, logging, and network policy considerations.

## Key Concepts

- **Namespace-scoped ConfigMaps**: Enable dynamic feature flags without pod restarts
- **InitContainers**: Provide bootstrap tooling (curl) before the main container starts
- **Conditional sidecars**: Driven by ConfigMap values to enable canary deployments
- **Readiness and liveness probes**: Ensure controller and application health
- **PVC-backed logs**: Provide persistent storage for debugging and audit trails
- **NetworkPolicies**: Enforce zero-trust networking by restricting egress to known endpoints

## Trade-offs

| Aspect | Consideration |
|--------|----------------|
| **Polling Interval** | Frequent polls increase API load; infrequent polls delay flag propagation |
| **ConfigMap Updates** | Applications must watch or periodically read the ConfigMap to detect changes |
| **Sidecar Overhead** | Running a sidecar even when disabled consumes resources; consider whether the main container can react to flag changes directly |
| **Egress Restriction** | Locking down NetworkPolicy requires knowing all upstream dependencies upfront |
| **Log Persistence** | PVCs add operational complexity and cost; consider external logging solutions for production |

## Minimal YAML Skeleton

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: feature-flags
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: feature-flags
  namespace: feature-flags
data:
  flags.json: '{}'
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: logs-pvc
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: flag-poller
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-poller
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: flag-poller
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-curl
          image: curlimages/curl:latest
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'cp /usr/bin/curl /tools/curl']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
      containers:
        - name: poller
          image: your-poller-image:latest
          command: ['/bin/sh', '-c', 'while true; do curl -s $FLAGS_API > /config/flags.json; sleep 60; done']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
        - name: sidecar
          image: your-sidecar-image:latest
          env:
            - name: FEATURE_ENABLED
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: feature-flags
                  key: enabled
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: feature-flags
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: flags-egress-policy
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-poller
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: flags-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
```

This design balances flexibility with operational simplicity, making it well-suited for Kubernetes feature management in multi-tenant environments.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to coordinate InitContainers, sidecars, and config-driven apps in CKAD. Ensures proper volume mounting, file-based reloading semantics, and safe network posture.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer: pre-flight yamllint validation of /configs
- Config mounting: PVC-backed /configs shared with main container and sidecar
- Sidecar watcher: detects changes and triggers in-app reload via /reload/trigger
- Readiness/Liveness probes: ensure proper pod health
- Namespace NetworkPolicy: restricts egress to internal services only

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton (Deployment)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-reloader
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-reloader
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: lint-configs
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "yamllint /configs/**/*.yaml || exit 1"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-volume
          mountPath: /configs
      containers:
      - name: main-app
        image: myapp:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-volume
          mountPath: /configs
        - name: reload-volume
          mountPath: /reload
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        env:
        - name: RELOAD_PATH
          value: /reload/trigger
      - name: reload-watcher
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "inotifywait -m /configs -e modify,create -e moved_to | while read; do touch /reload/trigger; done"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-volume
          mountPath: /configs
        - name: reload-volume
          mountPath: /reload
      volumes:
      - name: config-volume
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: config-pvc
      - name: reload-volume
        emptyDir: {}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you add multi-namespace isolation for this pattern?
- What happens on YAML syntax error after initial validation?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical security hardening and disruption management capabilities for CKAD-level Kubernetes deployments.

## Key Concepts
- Container SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem for container isolation
- PodSecurityContext: fsGroup for proper file permissions on PVC-mounted volumes
- Kernel capabilities: drop ALL to minimize attack surface
- PodDisruptionBudget: maintain minimum healthy pods during maintenance
- Rollout and rollback procedures for safe deployments

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
  labels:
    app: api-gateway
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api-gateway
    spec:
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 1001
      containers:
      - name: api-gateway
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 10001
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - "ALL"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /srv
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/app
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: api-gateway-pvc
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: api-gateway-config
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api-gateway-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-gateway
```

## Verification & Rollback
```bash
# Verify under load
kubectl exec deployment/api-gateway -- curl http://localhost:8080/health
kubectl top pods -l app=api-gateway
kubectl get pods -l app=api-gateway --watch

# Rollback if needed
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-gateway
kubectl rollout status deployment/api-gateway
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Matters
This question tests critical CKAD competencies: initializing pods with InitContainers, configuring volume mounts for data sharing, implementing zero-downtime deployments, and ensuring availability during disruptions with PodDisruptionBudgets.

## Key Concepts

- **InitContainer**: Runs to completion before main containers start. Uses the same volume mounts to share data with the main container. Multiple init containers run sequentially.

- **Volume Mounts**: The ConfigMap is mounted at `/config` for the init container to access `cache-base`. An `emptyDir` volume shares `/var/cache` between init and main containers.

- **RollingUpdate maxUnavailable: 0**: Critical for zero-downtime updates. Ensures all 3 pods update one at a time, with a new pod fully ready before the old one terminates.

- **PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable: 2**: With 3 replicas, guarantees at least 2 pods remain healthy during voluntary disruptions (node drains, API server issues). This prevents service degradation.

## Common Pitfalls

1. **Missing volumeMounts in init container** - InitContainer cannot access volumes without explicit mountPath
2. **maxUnavailable set to 1** - Can cause brief unavailability during rolling updates
3. **PDB selector mismatch** - Must match the Deployment's pod selector exactly
4. **Forgetting emptyDir for /var/cache** - Without a volume, /var/cache would be lost on container restart

## Why This Is Asked
This tests practical CKAD skills: using Kubernetes CSR API, namespace-scoped Secrets, and security controls in a rotation workflow.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes CertificateSigningRequest, automated approval, private CA
- Secrets and Secret Mounts, TLS configuration in Pods
- InitContainers and container probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting CA access
- RBAC implications and audit considerations

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal CronJob skeleton that triggers TLS rotation
# (Note: actual CSR creation is performed by a script in the container)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: tls-rotate
spec:
  schedule: "*/30 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: tls-rotate-sa
          containers:
          - name: rotate
            image: bitnami/kubectl
            command: ["/bin/sh","-c","kubectl certificate approve csr-service-tls-rotation"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to design an isolated TLS rotation workflow that leverages cert-manager, RBAC, and policy enforcement while producing auditable logs.

## Key Concepts
- Deployments, InitContainers, and probes for reliable pod lifecycle management
- Secrets and Bearer token authentication for secure credential handling
- cert-manager integration for automated certificate rotation testing
- PVC-based logging for persistent audit trails
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control and network segmentation

## Trade-offs
- **Simplicity vs. Security**: Using a single ServiceAccount with broad permissions simplifies implementation but increases blast radius if compromised
- **PVC vs. Sidecar**: A sidecar container offers simpler log shipping but adds resource overhead; a PVC requires external log rotation
- **Polling vs. Watching**: Polling with a cron-style schedule is less efficient than watching but avoids the complexity of setting up a custom controller with informers
- **Egress Control**: NetworkPolicy adds security but increases operational complexity and requires CNI support

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
  namespace: cert-verifier
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
  namespace: cert-verifier
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["cert-manager.io"]
    resources: ["certificates"]
    verbs: ["get", "create", "delete"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
  namespace: cert-verifier
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: cert-verifier
    namespace: cert-verifier
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: cert-verifier
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-credentials
  namespace: cert-verifier
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: "<bearer-token>"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier-logs
  namespace: cert-verifier
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier
  namespace: cert-verifier
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cert-verifier
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cert-verifier
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: cert-verifier
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: alpine:latest
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - apk add --no-cache curl jq
          volumeMounts:
            - name: workdir
              mountPath: /work
      containers:
        - name: verifier
          image: alpine:latest
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              apk add --no-cache curl jq
              while true; do
                # Watch secrets, check expiry, rotate, post digest
                sleep 3600
              done
          volumeMounts:
            - name: workdir
              mountPath: /work
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /var/log
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthy
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: workdir
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: cert-verifier-logs
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: cert-verifier-egress
  namespace: cert-verifier
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cert-verifier
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              name: audit-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: audit-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

## Why This Is Asked
Auditors assess knowledge of Kubernetes pod security hardening and defense-in-depth strategies.

## Key Concepts
- Pod securityContext vs container securityContext
- runAsNonRoot enforcement and UID requirements
- readOnlyRootFilesystem and volume mount implications
- Capability dropping and privilege escalation controls
- Seccomp profiles via annotations and runtime defaults
- Rolling update safety and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```yaml
# Security hardening patch for collector Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod: runtime/default
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 2000
      containers:
      - name: collector
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL
          volumeMounts:
          - name: input
            mountPath: /data/input
          - name: output
            mountPath: /data/output
        # Preserve existing probes and resources
        # livenessProbe, readinessProbe, resources remain unchanged
```

## Validation & Rollback
**Validation:**
- `kubectl get pods -n apps -l app=collector -o yaml | grep securityContext`
- `kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:apps:collector`
- Test pod startup and volume access
- Verify non-root execution: `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- id`

**Rollback:**
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/collector -n apps`
- Monitor rollout status: `kubectl rollout status deployment/collector -n apps`
- Document security context changes in version control

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical CKAD skills: wiring ConfigMaps and Secrets, configuring InitContainers, implementing TLS sidecars, setting up readiness/liveness probes, and crafting a NetworkPolicy with conditional egress.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap-driven feature flags
- Secrets for credential management
- InitContainers for tooling installation
- TLS sidecars for secure communication
- Readiness and liveness probe configuration
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: feature-config
data:
  ENABLE_API: "true"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: api-creds
type: Opaque
data:
  token: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: app-namespace
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-policy
  namespace: app-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: internal-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: app-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: curlimages/curl:latest
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo Initialized']
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: my-app:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: ENABLE_API
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: feature-config
                  key: ENABLE_API
            - name: API_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: api-creds
                  key: token
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /status
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /status
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
        - name: tls-sidecar
          image: nginx:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 443
```

## Trade-offs
- **NetworkPolicy complexity**: The policy above allows egress only to the internal-api pod. A more permissive approach might allow DNS resolution but restrict target services.
- **InitContainer overhead**: Installing curl in every pod increases startup time and image size. Consider baking tools into the base image if startup latency is critical.
- **Sidecar maintenance**: A TLS sidecar adds complexity and resource overhead. For simple use cases, TLS could be handled within the application container directly.
- **Secret security**: Storing credentials in a Secret is fine for basic scenarios, but consider external secrets operators or vault integration for production environments requiring rotation.
- **Probe configuration**: Aggressive probe settings can cause unnecessary restarts; conservative settings may delay failure detection. Tune based on application startup time.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to extend a deployment with a sidecar, config-driven validation, and observability while preserving availability.

## Key Concepts
- Sidecar patterns, config-driven validation, and health checks
- Rolling updates triggered by ConfigMap changes via checksum/config
- Resource limits, preStop lifecycle, and PodDisruptionBudget
- Load testing and safe rollback strategies

## Code Example
```yaml
# Patch sketch for ingest deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ingest
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "$(kubectl get configmap ingestrules -o json | sha256sum)"
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: ingest
          image: ingest:latest
          resources:
            requests: {"cpu": "100m", "memory": "128Mi"}
            limits: {"cpu": "250m", "memory": "256Mi"}
        - name: validator
          image: validator:latest
          ports: [{"containerPort": 9000}]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
          resources:
            requests: {"cpu": "100m", "memory": "128Mi"}
            limits: {"cpu": "250m", "memory": "256Mi"}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: "/healthz", port: 9000}
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: "/readyz", port: 9000}
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["sleep", "5"]
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: ingest-data-pvc
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: ingestrules
```

```yaml

apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget

spec:

```

## Why This Is Asked

- InitContainer bootstraps config from central API
- Sidecar monitors config changes and signals main app
- Secrets for API tokens and credentials
- Shared volume for config sync
- PVC for logs and /logs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to config API

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-reload
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: config
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-claim
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: your-app:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /var/log/app
        - name: reloader
          image: myorg/config-reloader:latest
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 300; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
```
